activities.caption: rebuild the tuner chain, factor by factor
activities.name: ueOrderTuners

config.prompt: The classic piano-tuner estimate — put the decomposition chain in order:
items: 3 million metro residents, say 1 million households
1 household in 5 owns a piano: about 200,000 pianos
Each piano tuned about once a year: 200,000 tunings per year
One tuner does about 1,000 tunings a year (4 a day, 5 days, 50 weeks)
200,000 ÷ 1,000 ≈ 200 tuners — within a factor of 2 of the Yellow Pages count
config.why: Six guessable factors, each debatable by a factor of 3, and the chain still lands within one order of magnitude — independent errors partially cancel.

activities.anchor: The imperial system muddies this deliberately
activities.caption: fill the blanks — mass, weight and the pounds trap
activities.name: ueMassCloze

config.text: The SI system separates %%0%% (quantity of matter — identical on the Moon) from weight, the gravitational force on it. In imperial units the %%1%% (lbm) and %%2%% (lbf) coincide on Earth's surface only because the conversion constant gc happens to equal g — write F = ma without dividing by gc and you are off by that factor everywhere gravity is not Earth-standard.
config.hint: The lesson's whole disasters section hangs on this one distinction.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the scale on the Moon
activities.name: ueMoonPredict

config.q: A 70 kg person steps on a bathroom scale on the Moon, where surface gravity is about a sixth of Earth's. What number does the display show?
choices: About 12 kg — it is a force meter doing arithmetic in newtons wherever it sits
The display goes blank — there is no gravity in space
config.why: The scale reads the gravitational force (about 114 N up there) and divides by 9.81 to display kilograms — so the same 70 kg of matter shows a sixth of the number, without a gram of matter changing.

activities.anchor: The price of carelessness is on the record
activities.caption: pair each failure with its unit error
activities.name: ueDisasterMatch

config.prompt: Two lost missions, one lost check — pair them:

pairs.right: thruster impulse read in pound-force-seconds where navigation expected newton-seconds — a factor of 4.45 at every burn
fuel load computed in pounds where the metric 767 needed kilograms — 17 minutes of glide to a disused airbase
why pound-mass and pound-force coincide on Earth's surface only

config.why: Both failures were caught by no one at any stage because nobody performed the check that takes ten seconds — dimensional checking at every line would have saved both missions.

activities.caption: someone sneers at your 10× estimate — walk the decision
activities.name: ueGateBranch

config.root: Your estimate is within an order of magnitude, and a reviewer objects: 'It could be 10× off.'

start.text: What does the estimate actually buy the project?

choices.label: It sorts feasible from absurd — and gates the design
choices.feedback: The estimate's real job: the decision, made in minutes.

choices.label: It replaces the detailed analysis
choices.feedback: Not so — analysis can and must follow.

choices.label: It pins down the exact number
choices.feedback: Estimates are sorting devices, not measuring devices.

gate.text: 10 kg of battery or 1,000 kg? A 10-metre bridge or a 100-metre bridge? Detailed analysis follows — but only for the option the estimate allowed to pass.

replace.text: The estimate gates everything, then hands the surviving option to the full analysis — precision applied to the wrong order of magnitude is wasted precision.

exact.text: A design wrong by 100× will not be rescued by precision — and an estimate never manufactures precision it did not earn.

config.why: The estimate is the gate, not the substitute: it sorts feasible from absurd for free, and everything past the gate is earned digit by digit.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — deriving the pendulum period
activities.name: uePendulumSpot

config.prompt: A student's dimensional derivation of the pendulum contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The period T can depend only on length L, mass m and gravity g.
The only combination of L and g that yields seconds is √(L/g).
Mass enters through the weight, so heavier pendulums swing faster.
Scaling the length up 10× multiplies the period by about √10.
Experiment or derivation must supply the dimensionless constant, 2π.
config.correction: Mass cannot enter at all — no combination of metres and m/s² makes kilograms cancel; every mass swings alike.
config.why: Dimensional analysis fixes the form T = 2π√(L/g) and kills m outright; the 2π is a pure number, invisible to unit bookkeeping.

activities.anchor: No amount of unit bookkeeping can produce a pure number
activities.caption: file each result: delivered by dimensions, or earned elsewhere
activities.name: ueFormBuckets

config.prompt: Dimensional analysis delivers the form — file each prize:
buckets: must come from experiment or derivation

items.label: T ∝ √(L/g) — which quantities combine and how they scale
F ∝ ρv²A — the quadratic drag's form
strength scales with length², weight with length³
the constants inside the drag law

config.why: It delivers the form, never the number: experiment or derivation has to supply the constant.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — how far can the error spread?
activities.name: ueErrorEstimate

config.prompt: A quantity is computed from three measurements, each good to about 1%. Roughly what total uncertainty should you quote?
config.why: The three 1% inputs compound: 1% + 1% + 1% ≈ 3% — everything past that is noise in a suit.
config.context: Ask any spreadsheet jockey quoting seven decimals from three input numbers each known to 5%.
